- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.5) in recent days, model tends to overcorrect downward; reduce forecast dip depth or add slight upward bias.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >+5% from prior peak), model often overshoots and fails to mean-revert; cap forecast peak and introduce early downward slope.
- If sentiment is positive but price is trending down, model often ignores sentiment and forecasts continuation; align forecast with sentiment direction even if price is falling.
- Model frequently underestimates true price volatility in early forecast windows (e.g., 30d) — especially when sentiment is volatile — increase forecast range or add 1–2% buffer for uncertainty.
- When sentiment history shows repeated negative swings, model tends to lag in recognizing reversal — delay forecast rebound until sentiment turns positive or price shows clear momentum.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, model often overestimates mean reversion — adjust downward by 0.5–1.5% if sentiment is neutral or mildly positive.
- If sentiment is consistently low (e.g., < -0.3 for 5+ days), model tends to forecast lower than true — add 0.5–1.0% upward bias to counteract pessimism bias.
- Avoid forecasting sharp upward moves when sentiment is mixed or negative — model often overreacts; cap forecast rise at 2–3% above recent peak unless sentiment is strongly bullish.
